title: The Prayer of a Pagan
text:
Do not let your flames die;

Warm my deaf heart,

Voluptuousness, cruel torment!

Diva! supplicem exaudî!


Goddess diffused in the air,

Flame of our underground,

Listen to a consumed soul

That raises to you its iron song,


Voluptuousness, be my queen!

Take on a siren's mask

Made of flesh and brocade,


Or pour your deep dreams into me

In the shapeless and mystical liquor,

Voluptuousness, elastic phantom!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the pagan invocation, including the Latin plea and the repeated address to Voluptuousness.

title: The Cat
text:
Come, beautiful cat, to my loving breast;

Hold back the claws of your paw,

And let me sink into your lovely eyes,

A mixture of agate and metal.


While my fingers softly comb

Your head and your elastic back,

While my hand grows drunk with pleasure

Touching your electric body,


I think I see my lady. Her gaze,

Like yours, amiable beast,

Deep and cold, wounds like a dart,


And, from feet to head,

A subtle air, a dangerous scent,

Sail around her tawny body.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sensual comparison between the cat's gaze/body and the beloved's dangerous presence.

title: Love and the Skull
text:
Love sits on the skull

Of Humanity,

And on such a throne the profane one,

With lewd laughter,


Cheerfully blows round bubbles,

Which rise in the air,

As if to join the worlds

At the depths of Ether.


The luminous and fragile globe,

In a wide flight,

Bursts and spits out its little soul

Like a golden dream.


And I hear the skull, at each bubble,

Pray and moan:

"This fierce and ridiculous fire,

When will it end?


For what your cruel mouth

Scatters in the air,

Murderous monster, is my brain,

My blood and my flesh!"
editorial_note: The translation preserves the grotesque allegory of Love blowing bubbles from humanity's skull.

title: The Death of Lovers
text:
We will possess beds heaped with aromas

And, like tombs, very deep divans,

And strange flowers on the consoles,

Our own, that burst in warmer skies.


Stirring final ardors to the limit,

Both hearts will be two torches

Whose indistinct lights will be reflected

In our two souls, one day twin.


And, at last, on a rose and mystic blue evening,

We will exchange a single lightning flash

Like a sob heavy with farewells.


And later, an Angel, half-opening doors,

Will come to revive, faithful and joyful,

The clouded mirrors and the dead flames.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the lovers' death chamber as sensual, funereal, and finally revived by the angel.

title: The Stranger
text:
"Whom do you love best, enigmatic man, tell me, your father, your mother, your sister, or your brother?"


"I have neither father, nor mother, nor sister, nor brother."


"Your friends?"


"You use a word whose meaning, to this day, I have not come to know."


"Your homeland?"


"I do not know in what latitude it is situated."


"Beauty?"


"Gladly would I love her, since she is goddess and immortal."


"Gold?"


"I abhor it as you abhor God."


"Then whom do you love, extraordinary stranger?"


"I love the clouds... the clouds that pass... over there... the marvelous clouds!"
editorial_note: The translation preserves the catechism-like dialogue and the stranger's final devotion to passing clouds.
